headline: The Orthopedics Foundation
threshold: By Lesson 10, you can greet patients, name basic body parts and supplies, ask simple history questions, give clear exam commands, ask for an interpreter, and start Orthopedics Lesson 1.

lessons.title: Sounds and Greetings
lessons.objective: Greet a patient, say who you are, and pronounce basic body and clinic words clearly.
lessons.focus: The five pure vowels, ch, j, ll, rr, silent h and the written accent; greetings

words.note: The h is silent; hue sounds like 'weh': WEH-so.
ll sounds like English y in Mexico: ro-DEE-ya.
The written accent puts the stress on í: ra-dio-gra-FEE-a.
Sounds like YEH-so.
ie sounds like 'yeh': PYEHR-na.
In Latin America z sounds like s: BRA-so.
Feminine even though it ends in -o.
ñ sounds like ny in 'canyon'.
Spanish vowels are short and pure: KO-do.
ch sounds like English ch in 'church'.
Trill the r at the start of ruedas, like rr.
j sounds like a strong English h: heh-REEN-ga.

words.es: Buenos días, soy el doctor Rivera.
words.note: Use until noon. A woman says soy la doctora.

words.en: Nice to meet you, Mrs. García.

words.note: Usted is formal; use it with every patient.

words.en: Good afternoon, come in and sit down, please.
words.es: Buenas tardes, pase y siéntese, por favor.
words.note: Buenas tardes is used from noon until dark.

words.es: Hasta luego, que le vaya bien.

lessons.speaking: Greet a patient at the clinic, say your name, and point to the knee, arm and hand as you say each word clearly.

lessons.title: Numbers, Time and Measurements
lessons.objective: Say numbers, appointment times, weeks, pounds and degrees with patients and staff.
lessons.focus: Numbers 0 to 1,000, a las for clock time, and weeks, pounds, degrees and mm with de

words.note: Masculine even though it ends in -a.
Used for range of motion and angles.
X-ray measurements are usually in mm.
US clinics weigh patients in pounds.
Use son las for every hour except 1: es la 1.

words.es: Su cita es el lunes a las 10:30.
words.note: Say a las diez y media.
Measurements take de: es de 180 libras.

words.en: The prescription says 1 pill every 8 hours.
words.es: La receta dice 1 pastilla cada 8 horas.
words.note: Always read the dose from the prescription or the order.

lessons.speaking: Tell a patient the day and time of their next appointment, how many weeks until they come back, and read their weight in pounds.

lessons.title: Ser and Estar
lessons.objective: Say who you are and describe a patient's condition or location with ser and estar.
lessons.focus: ser for identity and job (soy cirujano), estar for condition and location (está hinchada)

words.note: Agrees with the noun: la rodilla está hinchada.
Patients say roto for a broken bone.
Literally purple; patients use it for a bruise.
A woman is la paciente.
A man is el enfermero.
A woman says cirujana ortopedista. No article after ser for a job.

words.en: The knee is swollen and bruised.
words.es: La rodilla está hinchada y morada.
words.note: estar: a condition that can change.

words.en: The nurse is in the operating room.
words.es: La enfermera está en el quirófano.
words.note: estar for location.
ser for what something is or when it is from.

lessons.speaking: Introduce yourself to a nurse as an orthopedic surgeon and describe a patient's knee: swollen, bruised, sore or stable.

lessons.title: Have, There Is, Need and Want
lessons.objective: Ask what a patient has or wants and say what they need: crutches, a sling or ice.
lessons.focus: tener, hay, necesitar, querer, and hay que + infinitive for what must be done

words.note: Common in Mexico; also la manta.

words.en: Are you allergic to any medication?
Ice needs to go on the ankle.
words.es: Hay que poner hielo en el tobillo.
words.note: hay que + infinitive: what must be done, with no subject.

words.en: There is a nurse here to help you.
words.es: Hay una enfermera aquí para ayudarle.
words.note: hay: there is / there are.

words.en: I have the results of your X-ray.
words.es: Tengo los resultados de su radiografía.

lessons.speaking: Ask a patient if they have allergies or a fever, and tell them what they need: crutches, a sling, a splint or ice.

lessons.title: Go, Do and Can
lessons.objective: Tell a patient what you are going to do and ask what they can move or do.
lessons.focus: ir a + infinitive for plans, hacer for what you do, poder + infinitive to ask ability

words.note: Los dedos del pie are the toes.

words.en: I'm going to check your knee now.
words.es: Voy a revisar su rodilla ahora.
words.note: ir a + infinitive: a plan.

words.en: We're going to take an X-ray of the hand.
words.es: Vamos a tomar una radiografía de la mano.

words.en: Tomorrow you are going to go to physical therapy.
words.es: Mañana usted va a ir a terapia física.

words.note: hacer: hago, hace, hacemos.

words.en: Can you climb the stairs at home?

lessons.speaking: Tell a patient what you are going to do today: check the knee, take an X-ray, and send them to physical therapy tomorrow.

lessons.title: Present Tense
lessons.objective: Talk about daily clinic and OR work and ask patients simple present-tense questions.
lessons.focus: Regular -ar, -er, -ir endings: trabajo, camina, operamos, escriben, vive

words.note: Common in Mexico for the patient's chart.
A woman is la residente.

words.en: I work at this clinic on Mondays.
words.es: Trabajo en esta clínica los lunes.

words.en: Do you live alone or with your family?
words.es: ¿Usted vive solo o con su familia?
words.note: Ask a woman: ¿vive sola?

words.en: Do you walk with a cane?
Today we operate on Mr. López's hip.
words.es: Hoy operamos la cadera del señor López.
words.note: Present tense works for a plan today: operamos.
Tú with a coworker; use a before a person.

lessons.speaking: Ask a patient whether they live alone and walk with a cane, then tell a resident what you do on Mondays.

lessons.title: Questions
lessons.objective: Ask a patient where it hurts, when and how it happened, and what medicines they take.
lessons.focus: Question words qué, quién, dónde, cuándo, cuánto, cómo, por qué, cuál with le duele

words.note: Agrees with the noun: ¿cuántas pastillas?
Written apart for 'why'; porque together means 'because'.
Mexico often uses cuál before a noun: ¿cuál rodilla?
Patients say golpe for any hit or bump.
le duele: it hurts you (formal).

words.en: Which knee hurts, the right or the left?
words.es: ¿Qué rodilla le duele, la derecha o la izquierda?
words.note: Use qué before a noun: ¿qué rodilla?

words.en: How many pills do you take a day?

lessons.speaking: Ask a patient where it hurts, when they fell, how it happened, which side it is, and what medicines they take.

lessons.title: No, Never and How Much
lessons.objective: Say what is not happening yet and compare pain or swelling: more, less, another.
lessons.focus: Negatives no, nunca, nadie, nada, todavía no, and comparing with más, menos, otro

words.note: Goes right before the verb: no puede.
Never put un before otro: otra radiografía.
Patients say se me duerme la mano for numbness.

words.en: You can't put weight on the foot yet.
words.es: Todavía no puede apoyar el pie.
words.note: apoyar el pie: to put weight on the foot.

words.en: Does it hurt more or less than yesterday?
words.es: ¿Le duele más o menos que ayer?

words.en: I need another X-ray of the ankle.
There's nobody in the operating room yet.
words.es: No hay nadie en el quirófano todavía.

words.en: You don't feel anything in your toes?
words.es: ¿No siente nada en los dedos del pie?
words.note: The double negative is correct: no... nada.

lessons.speaking: Ask a patient whether the pain and swelling are more or less than yesterday, then tell a nurse you need another X-ray.

lessons.title: Polite Requests and Commands
lessons.objective: Ask politely and give clear usted commands to guide a patient through a simple exam.
lessons.focus: ¿Puede + infinitive? and usted commands with attached pronouns: póngase, acuéstese

words.note: Common in US Spanish; also el formulario.

words.en: Can you take off your shoes, please?
words.note: ¿Puede...? is the softest way to ask.
Usted command; the pronoun attaches: póngase.

words.en: Lie on your back on the exam table.
words.es: Acuéstese boca arriba en la camilla.

lessons.speaking: Guide a patient through a short exam: ask them to take off their shoes, put on the gown, lie face up and bend the knee slowly.

lessons.title: Words You Already Know and Getting Help
lessons.objective: Recognize medical cognates and use survival phrases when you don't understand.
lessons.focus: Cognates ending in -ción, -dad and -ente, plus survival phrases for getting help

words.note: -ción words are feminine: la operación.
-dad words are feminine: la movilidad.
A woman is la intérprete.

words.en: Can you repeat more slowly, please?
I'm going to call an interpreter.
words.es: Voy a llamar a un intérprete.
words.note: Use a before a person: llamar a un intérprete.

words.en: How do you say this in Spanish?
It's urgent, I need help here.

lessons.speaking: Tell a patient you speak a little Spanish, ask them to repeat more slowly, and say you are going to call an interpreter.
